The three-body problem of this course moved three bodies under gravity: every
pair attracts in proportion to the product of its masses and the inverse
square of its distance. Change the world, and nothing of the method changes.
The bodies still pull or push each other along the lines between them, the
forces of a pair are still equal and opposite, and the motion is still found
by integrating Newton's second law. What changes is the law of the pair: its
strength, its sign, and how fast it falls with distance. A world of charged
bodies has couplings that are not their masses; a world in another number of
dimensions has another exponent.

This lesson puts a language model in such a world. Three bodies of known
masses interact through pair forces whose **couplings and exponent are
hidden**. The model may place the bodies at rest anywhere in a box and read
their accelerations, with noise. It must state the three couplings and the
exponent. The build then sets the bodies **moving**, from starts the model
never saw, some of them outside the box, integrates the motion under the
claimed law and under the hidden one, and compares the positions. The claim
is scored by what it predicts, not by what it fits.

## Assumptions

1. **The world is simulated, and its law is in the family.** The force of the
   pair $i, j$ is $k_{ij}\,r_{ij}^{-p}$ along the line between them, positive
   for attraction, with one exponent $p$ for every pair (`PairForceWorld` of
   `pbc.discovery.worlds`). Newton's gravity is the case
   $k_{ij} = G\,m_i m_j$, $p = 2$, and the accelerations then equal those of the
   N-body model of this course (`pbc.mechanics.nbody`), which a test checks.
2. **The truth is out of reach.** The couplings, the exponent, and the
   held-out starts are in no tool, prompt, or page. A test shows that no tool
   description, prompt, or public attribute contains them, and that no tool
   reaches the judge. The page prints claims and their scores.
3. **The predictive test.** From each held-out start the bodies are integrated
   by the adaptive Dormand-Prince method of order eight at a tight tolerance,
   and their positions are compared at four times up to four seconds. The
   error is the root-mean-square position error divided by the
   root-mean-square distance of the bodies from their centre of mass. The claim
   is **recovered** when it is at most `{python} result["tolerance"]`.
4. **The rules came before the run.** The world, the starts, the budget, and
   the tolerance were fixed in `pbc.discovery.world_lab` before the run was
   recorded. The condition is **`{python} result["condition"]`**: the agent is
   told the form of the pair force, not its couplings or exponent.
5. **The agent is untrusted and its words are data.** The score is a function
   of its tool calls.

## Reading a pair force from a still picture {#explanation}

At rest, the acceleration of body $i$ is the sum of the pulls of the other
two, each divided by its mass:

$$
\mathbf{a}_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j \ne i} k_{ij}\, r_{ij}^{-p}\,
\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{ij},
\qquad \hat{\mathbf{r}}_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i}{r_{ij}}.
$$

Six numbers come back per configuration, and four are unknown, so one
configuration could in principle determine them; in practice the noise and
the coupling of the unknowns call for several. A configuration chosen with
care makes the arithmetic simple. Put the first body at a corner, the second
along one axis and the third along the other: the pull of the second on the
first is then purely along the first axis and that of the third purely along
the second, so each
component of $\mathbf{a}_1$ measures one coupling at one distance. Two such
configurations with different distances give the exponent from a ratio,
$p = \ln(a/a')/\ln(r'/r)$.

**Static readings, dynamic test.** A law found from bodies at rest is tested
on bodies in motion. The motion integrates the force over many
configurations and over time, so a small error in a coupling or the exponent
becomes a drift in position that grows. The predictive test reads that
drift.

### What the agent may and may not do

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.display("allowlist")
```

The agent may call `accelerations` at most `{python} result["budget"]` times
and `submit` to state its claim, in at most `{python} result["max-steps"]`
messages of at most `{python} result["max-calls"]` tool calls each, and write
text. It may not run code, read a file, reach the network, or call the judge.

## Worked examples

### Baselines without a model

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.the_baselines)
```

```{python}
#| label: d5-baselines
#| echo: false
result.table("d5-baselines")
```

[Least squares of the family on random configurations predicts the motion
within the tolerance; Newton's gravity and a sparse sum of whole powers of the
distance fail the chi-square and the prediction.]{.claim
type="numerically-verified" scope="the simulated world, one seed, the
protocol's budget of random configurations, the held-out starts"
evidence="d5-baselines"} The world is not gravity: its couplings are not
proportional to the products of the masses, and the fitted exponent is not
two. The sparse sum shows a subtler failure:

```{python}
#| label: d5-sparse
#| echo: false
result.table("d5-sparse")
```

It approximates a fractional power by a difference of whole powers, and the
threshold dropped one pair's coupling altogether because it was smaller than
a fifth of the largest coefficient. A method that can only state whole
powers cannot state this world.

The agent spent a third of the budget that the baselines spent. One run says

### The predictive test in time

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.draw_predictive_test)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-predictive-test
#| echo: false
#| fig-status: simulated
#| fig-cap: "Position error relative to the size of the system against time on the held-out starts. The agent's claim and the least-squares fit stay orders of magnitude below the tolerance; Newton's gravity and the sparse sum of whole powers cross it within the first two seconds."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with a logarithmic vertical axis of relative position error against time from zero to four seconds. Four rising curves: the agent's and the least-squares fit lie close together far below a dashed tolerance line; the sparse identification and Newton's gravity curves start higher and cross the tolerance line early, ending well above it."
result.show("fig-predictive-test")
```

The motions are simulated and recomputed by this build; the held-out starts
are not drawn, since they are the judge's. Every error grows with time,
because an error in the force accumulates into an error of velocity and then
of position. [A wrong law fails the test within the first two seconds, while
the claims of the right family stay more than ten times below the tolerance
over the whole four seconds.]{.claim type="numerically-verified" scope="the
simulated world, the held-out starts, four seconds" evidence="fig-predictive-test
d5-comparison"} Over a longer time, or near a close encounter, even small
errors would grow faster: three bodies can be chaotic, as the three-body
lesson shows, and a predictive test of a chaotic system has a horizon.

### Run the agent yourself

This needs your own key and costs a few cents. The build does not run it, so
the commands are marked.

::: {.not-verified}
```bash
uv sync --locked --no-dev --extra openai
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."
cd site/lessons/agents-llm/15-unknown-physical-worlds
uv run --locked --no-dev --extra openai python -m pbc.discovery.world_lab
```
:::

A live run may use another design, misread a sign, or assume gravity. The
predictive test says which.

## Limits {#limits}

- **One run, one world.** The page shows one agent, once, in one world with
  one repulsive pair. It does not show that agents find unknown couplings in
  general, or with another prompt or condition.
- **The form was told.** The condition is `full`: the agent knew that the
  force is a power of the distance with one exponent for every pair. A world
  with another form, a force that depends on velocity, or a coupling of three
  bodies at once, cannot be claimed here.
- **A short, gentle horizon.** The held-out starts keep the bodies apart for
  four seconds. The test does not reach close encounters or long times, where
  small errors in the law would grow much faster.
- **Simulated, not observed.** Nothing here observes a physical system. Real
  astronomical N-body problems are observed, not probed: no one places stars
  at rest. The lesson isolates the inference from the observation.
- **The recording is not an API run.** It is a Claude Code session, told to
  answer in the harness's format and to use no tool of its own; the session
  reported no token count or price.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
An agent reads the accelerations of a few configurations, sees that every
body is pulled toward the others most of the time, and submits Newton's
gravity with a fitted $G$. Least squares of the family, on the same readings,
finds a repulsive pair. How should the run be reported?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
As a success, since gravity explains most of the readings.

::: {.feedback}
The score is the predictive error on the held-out starts, and gravity's error
exceeds the tolerance. "Most of the readings" is not a criterion the protocol
uses.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
As a failure, with its score: the chi-square of gravity is far beyond the
noise, and its predicted motion leaves the tolerance within seconds.

::: {.feedback}
Right. The baseline shows that the readings contained the repulsive pair;
the failure is the claim's.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
As inconclusive, because the world is unusual.

::: {.feedback}
The world and the test were fixed before the run. An unusual world is the
point of the test, not a reason to suspend it.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
As a failure. The familiar law does not describe the readings (its
chi-square is orders of magnitude above the noise) and does not predict the
motion. The least-squares baseline on the same budget shows that the
information was there, which is what makes the failure informative.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
Under Newton's gravity, each coupling divided by the product of the masses
of its pair is the same number, $G$. Divide the agent's couplings by the
products of the masses. Is this world gravity with other masses?

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.coupling_ratios)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("coupling-ratios")
```

The ratios differ between the pairs, and one is negative. No choice of $G$
makes them equal, and no choice of positive masses could either, since a
product of positive masses is positive. The bodies carry a property other
than their mass, which couples them, and in one pair it repels.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
How many configurations are needed? Fit the family by least squares to
random configurations with budgets from two to twelve configurations, and
score each fit by the predictive test.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.budget_scan)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("budget-scan")
```

Each configuration returns six numbers and the law has four unknowns, so two
configurations already over-determine it, and with this noise every budget
predicts the motion within the tolerance. A larger budget mostly lowers the
error further. With noisier readings, or a law with more unknowns, the
smallest sufficient budget would rise, and the predictive test is what would
show where.
:::
:::
